---
title: "Move from base R and stringr"
description: >
  The re_*() function for each base R and stringr function, and the
  places where the result differs.
---

```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
```

This guide is for someone who already matches regular expressions with
`grepl()`, `sub()` and `regmatches()`, or with stringr, and wants the
zuregex call that does the same. It gives the equivalents in two tables,
then shows the differences you would otherwise find by surprise.

```{r setup}
library(zuregex)
```

## The equivalent functions

Patterns that work in base R with `perl = TRUE` work unchanged: both use
PCRE2. stringr matches with ICU, whose syntax is close but not the same,
so check a pattern that uses anything beyond the common core.

| Task | Base R, `perl = TRUE` | stringr | zuregex |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Does it match? | `grepl()` | `str_detect()` | `re_detect()` |
| How many matches? | `lengths(gregexpr())` | `str_count()` | `re_count()` |
| Where is the first match? | `regexpr()` | `str_locate()` | `re_locate()` |
| Where is every match? | `gregexpr()` | `str_locate_all()` | `re_locate_all()` |
| The first match | `regmatches()` with `regexpr()` | `str_extract()` | `re_extract()` |
| Every match | `regmatches()` with `gregexpr()` | `str_extract_all()` | `re_extract_all()` |
| The groups of the first match | `regmatches()` with `regexec()`, `utils::strcapture()` | `str_match()` | `re_match()` |
| The groups of every match | `gregexec()` | `str_match_all()` | `re_match_all()` |
| Replace the first match | `sub()` | `str_replace()` | `re_replace(n = 1)` |
| Replace every match | `gsub()` | `str_replace_all()` | `re_replace()` |
| Split | `strsplit()` | `str_split()` | `re_split()` |
| Quote metacharacters | | `str_escape()` | `re_escape()` |

Base R's options become arguments that every `re_*()` function has.

| Base R | zuregex |
| --- | --- |
| `perl = TRUE` | always on |
| `ignore.case = TRUE` | `flags = "i"` |
| `fixed = TRUE` | `literal = TRUE` |
| `invert = TRUE` | `re_detect(negate = TRUE)` |
| `useBytes = TRUE` | a raw vector, or strings marked as `"bytes"` |

The subject comes first and the pattern second, as in stringr. With
`grepl()` and `sub()` it is the other way round.

```{r}
x <- c("2026-10-21 GET /index.html", "no date")
grepl("get", x, ignore.case = TRUE, perl = TRUE)
re_detect(x, "get", flags = "i")
```

## Replacement replaces every match

`re_replace()` is `gsub()`, not `sub()`: it replaces all the matches
unless `n` says otherwise. Compare the first two results, where only the
year changes, with the third.

```{r}
sub("\\d+", "#", x, perl = TRUE)
re_replace(x, "\\d+", "#", n = 1)
re_replace(x, "\\d+", "#")
```

## Templates use `$`, and know more

A replacement is a template in PCRE2's syntax, where a group is `$1` or
`${name}`. Base R writes `\\1` and stops at nine groups, with no names.
A base R template still works, since PCRE2 reads `\\1` to `\\9` as groups
too.

```{r}
sub("(\\d+)-(\\d+)", "\\2/\\1", x, perl = TRUE)
re_replace(x, "(?<year>\\d+)-(?<month>\\d+)", "${month}/${year}", n = 1)
```

A template can also give a default for a group that took no part in the
match. The second version has no minor number, so `${2:-0}` writes `0`.

```{r}
re_replace(c("v1.2", "v3"), "v(\\d+)(?:\\.(\\d+))?", "major $1, minor ${2:-0}")
```

`?re_replace` has the whole syntax, and replacement by a function.

## No match is `NA`, not a missing element

`regmatches()` drops the elements that did not match, so its result is
shorter than its input. `re_extract()` keeps one result per element.

```{r}
regmatches(x, regexpr("\\d+", x, perl = TRUE))
re_extract(x, "\\d+")
```

## Groups come back as a data frame

`str_match()` returns a character matrix whose first column is the whole
match. `re_match()` returns a data frame of the groups only, named after
them.

```{r}
stringr::str_match(x, "(?<year>\\d+)-(?<month>\\d+)")
re_match(x, "(?<year>\\d+)-(?<month>\\d+)")
```

With `proto` it does the work of `utils::strcapture()`, and the two calls
give the same typed data frame.

```{r}
proto <- data.frame(year = 0L, month = 0L)
utils::strcapture("(\\d+)-(\\d+)", x, proto, perl = TRUE)
re_match(x, "(\\d+)-(\\d+)", proto = proto)
```

## Patterns are never recycled

Base R uses only the first pattern of several, with a warning. zuregex
follows stringr: a pattern has length one or the length of `x`. Anything
else is an error, here three patterns for two strings.

```{r, error = TRUE}
re_detect(x, c("GET", "POST", "PUT"))
```

## Splitting keeps a trailing empty piece

`strsplit()` drops an empty string after the last separator. `re_split()`
keeps it, as Python's `re.split()` and `stringr::str_split()` do.

```{r}
strsplit("a,b,", ",", perl = TRUE)
re_split("a,b,", ",")
```

## See also

`?re_detect` describes the arguments every function shares. For the
reasons behind these choices, read
[Design and motivation](https://pedrobtz.github.io/zuregex/articles/design.html).
